name: Trader test battery, version 2
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries. Number sequences, probability at speed, and likelihood ranking with intervals.
description: These are reported formats from the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries, as described by Nov 2026. There are three papers, each on its own clock. Sequences is 15 questions in 25 minutes, one at a time, with no skipping. Probability at speed is 15 questions in 30 minutes; you may move between them. Likelihood ranking and intervals is 10 questions in 10 minutes. Wrong answers score 0, and no calculator is allowed. Firms mix and rename these papers, so expect a different order on the day. This is version 2 of 3.

items.title: That many times
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, ?

options.why: You moved on after one 4. Each number appears as many times as its value.
You went back to 3, which has already appeared three times.
You restarted the count. The runs only grow.

feedback.correct: Each number $n$ appears $n$ times.
feedback.generic: Count how often each number appears.

explain.text: Each number $n$ appears $n$ times: one 1, two 2s, three 3s. Only one 4 has appeared, so the next term is 4. Check: three more 4s follow before the first 5.

items.title: Blocks that count down
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4, 3, ?

options.why: You started a new block. The block from 4 counts down to 1 first.
You skipped 2. Each block counts down one step at a time.
You repeated 3. Each block falls by 1 each step.

feedback.correct: Blocks count down: 1; then 2, 1; then 3, 2, 1; then 4, 3, 2, 1.
feedback.generic: Split the terms into runs that end in 1.

explain.text: The terms fall into blocks 1; 2, 1; 3, 2, 1; and a block that starts at 4. That block has reached 3, so the next term is 2. Check: the block ends 2, 1, and then 5 starts the next.

items.title: Threes and fives
items.question: What comes next? 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, ?

options.why: 20 is a multiple of 5 and qualifies, but 18 comes first.
You added 2. 17 is a multiple of neither 3 nor 5.
You skipped 18, which is $3 \times 6$.

feedback.correct: These are the multiples of 3 or 5, in order.
feedback.generic: Ask what 3, 5, 6, 9 and 10 have in common, and look at 15.

explain.text: Every term is a multiple of 3 or of 5, listed in order, and 15, a multiple of both, is kept. After 15 come 16 and 17, which are neither, then $18 = 3 \times 6$. Check: the next after that is 20, a multiple of 5.

items.title: Squared primes
items.question: What comes next? 4, 9, 25, 49, 121, ?

options.why: You took the next square, $12^2$. The roots are primes, and 12 is not prime.
You skipped 13. After 11 the next prime is 13, so $13^2$ comes next.
You took one off $13^2$. The squares are exact.

feedback.correct: Each term is a prime squared: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, then 13.
feedback.generic: Take the square root of each term.

explain.text: The roots are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, the primes in order. The next prime is 13, so the next term is $13^2 = 169$. Check: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12 are missing from the roots, so the squares skip them.

items.title: Three to the place, plus the place
items.question: What comes next? 4, 11, 30, 85, 248, ?

options.why: You trebled 248. Each term is $3^n + n$, so trebling overshoots by 9.
You repeated the last gap of 163. The gaps nearly treble.
You added 5, the last place. The sixth term adds 6: $3^6 + 6 = 735$.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term is $3^n + n$.
feedback.generic: Subtract the powers of 3 from the terms.

explain.text: Take away 3, 9, 27, 81 and 243: you are left with 1 to 5, the term's place. So the sixth term is $3^6 + 6 = 735$. Check: each term is three times the one before, less 1, 3, 5, 7, then 9, and $3 \times 248 - 9 = 735$.

items.title: Halve or treble
items.question: What comes next? 7, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, ?

options.why: You used the odd rule on 52. An even term is halved.
You doubled 52. An even term is halved, not doubled.
You halved twice. Each step applies the rule once.

feedback.correct: Halve an even term; treble an odd term and add 1.
feedback.generic: Treat odd and even terms differently.

explain.text: An odd term $n$ goes to $3n + 1$, and an even term is halved: 7 gives 22, 22 gives 11, 11 gives 34. 52 is even, so the next term is 26. Check: 17 is odd and $3 \times 17 + 1 = 52$, as shown.

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 14. The gaps shrink.
You halved 70. The divisor rises by one each time.
You were one out. $420 \div 7 = 60$.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term is $420 \div n$.
feedback.generic: Divide 420 by each term.

explain.text: $420 \div 420 = 1$, $420 \div 210 = 2$, $420 \div 140 = 3$: the $n$th term is $420 \div n$. The seventh term is $420 \div 7 = 60$. Check: $70 \times 6 = 420$ and $60 \times 7 = 420$.

options.why: 24 qualifies, but 18 comes first.
20 has the factor 5. Every term is built from 2s and 3s only.
You doubled 16. $18 = 2 \times 3^2$ comes first.

feedback.correct: Numbers whose only prime factors are 2 and 3.
feedback.generic: Which numbers are missing, and why?

explain.text: 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 are missing, so the terms use no prime but 2 and 3. After 16, the next such number is $18 = 2 \times 3^2$. Check: 17 is prime, so nothing comes between 16 and 18.

items.title: Place times a power of two
items.question: What comes next? 2, 8, 24, 64, 160, ?

options.why: You doubled 160. The ratio falls each step: 4, 3, $\tfrac83$, $\tfrac52$.
You kept the last ratio of $\tfrac52$. The next ratio is $\tfrac{12}{5}$.
You repeated the last gap of 96. The gaps grow.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term is $n \times 2^n$.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by a power of 2.

explain.text: Dividing by 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 leaves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. So the sixth term is $6 \times 64 = 384$. Check: the ratio from 160 is $\tfrac{6}{5} \times 2 = 2.4$, and $160 \times 2.4 = 384$.

items.title: Squares in a mirror
items.question: What comes next? 1, 4, 9, 61, 52, 63, ?

options.why: You wrote $7^2$ the right way round. The terms reverse the digits.
You reversed 64. That is $8^2$; the next square is $7^2$.
You repeated the last gap of 11.

feedback.correct: The squares, with their digits reversed.
feedback.generic: Read 61, 52 and 63 backwards.

explain.text: 61, 52 and 63 are 16, 25 and 36 written backwards. The next square is 49, so the next term is 94. Check: 1, 4 and 9 read the same either way.

items.title: Multiply the two before
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 32, ?

options.why: You added the two before. Each term is their product.
You doubled 32. Multiply by the term before it, 8.
You squared 32. Multiply 32 by 8, not by itself.

feedback.correct: Each term is the product of the two before it.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with the two before it.

explain.text: $1 \times 2 = 2$, $2 \times 2 = 4$, $2 \times 4 = 8$, $4 \times 8 = 32$. So the next term is $8 \times 32 = 256$. Check: all terms are powers of 2 whose exponents 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 add like Fibonacci, and $3 + 5 = 8$ gives $2^8$.

items.title: A row of the triangle
items.question: What comes next? 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, ?

options.why: You jumped to the end. The row is symmetric, so 7 comes before the last 1.
You used row 6 of Pascal's triangle. This row starts 1, 7.
15 sits in row 6, not in this row.

feedback.correct: Row 7 of Pascal's triangle: $\binom{7}{k}$.
feedback.generic: Look for symmetry, and think of $\binom{n}{k}$.

explain.text: The terms are $\binom{7}{0}, \binom{7}{1}, \dots$: 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21. The next is $\binom{7}{6} = 7$. Check: the row reads the same backwards, so it mirrors the 7 near the start.

items.title: Two different primes
items.question: What comes next? 6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, ?

options.why: 25 is $5 \times 5$. Each term multiplies two different primes.
23 is prime. Each term is a product of two different primes.
33 is $3 \times 11$ and qualifies, but 26 comes first.

feedback.correct: Each term is the product of two different primes.
feedback.generic: Factorise each term.

explain.text: $6 = 2 \times 3$, $10 = 2 \times 5$, $14 = 2 \times 7$, $15 = 3 \times 5$, $21 = 3 \times 7$, $22 = 2 \times 11$. After 22, 23 is prime, 24 is $2^3 \times 3$ and 25 is $5^2$, so the next is $26 = 2 \times 13$. Check: 9 is missing because it is $3 \times 3$.

items.title: Add the mirror image
items.question: What comes next? 13, 44, 88, 176, 847, ?

options.why: You doubled 847. That works only when a term reads the same backwards.
You added 671, the reverse of the term before.
You were one out. $847 + 748 = 1595$.

feedback.correct: Each term is the one before plus its reverse.
feedback.generic: Read each term backwards.

items.title: Neighbouring primes
items.question: What comes next? 6, 15, 35, 77, 143, ?

options.why: You skipped 13. The pairs are neighbours: 11 and 13, then 13 and 17.
You doubled 143. Each term is a new pair of primes multiplied.
You used 15, which is not prime. After 13 the next prime is 17.

feedback.correct: Each term multiplies two neighbouring primes.
feedback.generic: Factorise 35, 77 and 143.

explain.text: $2 \times 3$, $3 \times 5$, $5 \times 7$, $7 \times 11$, $11 \times 13$: neighbouring primes multiplied. The next pair is 13 and 17, so the term is $13 \times 17 = 221$. Check: $13 \times 17 = 13 \times 15 + 26 = 195 + 26 = 221$.

items.title: A loaded die
items.question: A die is loaded so that 6 is twice as likely as each other face. The other five faces are equally likely. What is the chance of a 6?

options.why: You doubled $\tfrac16$. The chances must still add to 1.
You ignored the loading.
That is the chance of one of the other faces.

feedback.correct: Weights 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 and 2 add to 7, so a 6 has $\tfrac27$.
feedback.generic: Give each face a weight, then divide by the total weight.

explain.text: Give the five plain faces weight 1 and the 6 weight 2. The total is 7, so $P(6) = \tfrac27$. Check: the five other faces share $\tfrac57$, $\tfrac17$ each, half of $\tfrac27$.

items.title: Exactly one of two
items.question: Two trades are independent. One wins with chance $\tfrac14$, the other with chance $\tfrac13$. What is the chance that exactly one wins?

options.why: You added the two chances. That counts the case where both win.
That is the chance that at least one wins.
That is the chance that both win.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac23 + \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac{5}{12}$.
feedback.generic: Add the two ways: first wins and second loses, or the reverse.

explain.text: First wins alone: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac23 = \tfrac{2}{12}$. Second wins alone: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac13 = \tfrac{3}{12}$. Together $\tfrac{5}{12}$; check: at least one, $\tfrac12$, minus both, $\tfrac{1}{12}$, also gives $\tfrac{5}{12}$.

items.title: Four equal digits
items.question: A digital clock shows hours and minutes from 00:00 to 23:59. At a random minute of the day, what is the chance that all four digits are the same?

options.why: You counted 33:33, 44:44 and 55:55. The hours stop at 23.
You found only 00:00. 11:11 and 22:22 also work.
You let every digit run from 0 to 9. A clock has 1,440 minutes, not 10,000.

feedback.generic: List the times with four equal digits, then divide by the minutes in a day.

explain.text: Four equal digits need the hours to read 00, 11 or 22, and the minutes to match. That gives 3 of the $24 \times 60 = 1440$ minutes, so $\tfrac{3}{1440} = \tfrac{1}{480}$. Check: 33 is not an hour, so the list stops there.

items.title: Told it is odd
items.question: A whole number from 1 to 30 is picked at random. You are told it is odd. What is the chance it is prime?

options.why: You ignored the news: 10 of the 30 numbers are prime.
You counted 2 as an odd prime. Only 9 of the 15 odd numbers are prime.
You divided by all 30 numbers. Only the 15 odd ones remain.

feedback.correct: 9 of the 15 odd numbers are prime: $\tfrac35$.
feedback.generic: Keep only the odd numbers, then count the primes among them.

explain.text: There are 15 odd numbers. The odd primes are 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29, so $\tfrac{9}{15} = \tfrac35$. Check: $P(\text{prime and odd}) / P(\text{odd}) = \tfrac{9}{30} \div \tfrac{15}{30} = \tfrac35$.

items.title: One divides the other
items.question: Two whole numbers from 1 to 10 are picked at random and independently. What is the chance that the first divides the second exactly?

options.why: You left out the 10 pairs where the two are equal.
You counted only the pairs where the two are equal.
You stopped at a first number of 5. Each of 6 to 10 divides itself.

feedback.correct: First number $d$ divides $\lfloor 10/d \rfloor$ of the second numbers: 27 in all.
feedback.generic: Fix the first number and count its multiples up to 10.

explain.text: A first number $d$ divides $\lfloor 10/d \rfloor$ of the ten: 10, 5, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. These add to 27, so $\tfrac{27}{100}$. Check: counting by the second number, the factor counts 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 4, 3, 4 also add to 27.

items.title: A three-way stand-off
items.question: Three people play rock, paper, scissors, each choosing at random. There is no winner if all three choose the same or all three differ. What is the chance of no winner?

options.why: You counted only the cases where all three choose the same.
You counted only the cases where all three differ.
That is the chance there is a winner.

feedback.correct: 3 all-same plus 6 all-different outcomes, of 27.
feedback.generic: Count the all-same and all-different outcomes separately.

explain.text: All the same: 3 of the 27 outcomes. All different: $3! = 6$. So $\tfrac{9}{27} = \tfrac13$; check: two of one sign and one of another is $3 \times 2 \times 3 = 18$ outcomes, the other $\tfrac23$.

items.title: A rising PIN
items.question: A 4-digit PIN is picked at random from 0000 to 9999. What is the chance its digits strictly rise from left to right?

options.why: You divided by $4!$, but many PINs repeat a digit.
That is the chance the four digits all differ.
You counted PINs that rise or fall.

feedback.correct: Each set of 4 digits gives one rising PIN: $\binom{10}{4} = 210$ of 10,000.
feedback.generic: Pick which four digits appear. How many orders rise?

explain.text: Choose 4 different digits in $\binom{10}{4} = 210$ ways; exactly one order rises. So $\tfrac{210}{10{,}000} = \tfrac{21}{1000}$. Check: all digits differ in 5,040 PINs, and $\tfrac{1}{24}$ of those rise, which is 210.

items.title: Reds at both ends
items.question: Two red and three blue counters are laid in a row in random order. What is the chance that the two reds are at the two ends?

options.why: You treated the ends as independent, each red with chance $\tfrac25$.
That is the chance that the left end is red.
You fixed which red goes on the left. Either can.

feedback.correct: The reds take 2 of the 5 places, $\binom52 = 10$ ways, and one is both ends.
feedback.generic: Only the places of the reds matter.

explain.text: The two reds take 2 of 5 places, and the $\binom52 = 10$ choices are equally likely. One choice is both ends, so $\tfrac{1}{10}$. Check: left end red $\tfrac25$, then right end red $\tfrac14$, and $\tfrac25 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{10}$.

items.title: Digits that add to 3
items.question: A whole number from 100 to 999 is picked at random. What is the chance that its digits add to 3?

options.why: You allowed a first digit of 0, as in 030, and counted 000 to 999.
You missed 111.
You counted only 102, 111 and 120, the ones that start with 1.

feedback.generic: List them by their first digit.

explain.text: First digit 1 gives 102, 111 and 120; 2 gives 201 and 210; 3 gives 300. That is 6 of 900, or $\tfrac{1}{150}$; check: splitting 2 among three places after taking 1 from the first gives $\binom42 = 6$.

items.title: Paired up
items.question: Six people are split at random into three pairs. What is the chance that two named people end up as a pair?

options.why: You took 1 of the 3 pairs. What matters is who joins the first person.
You took 1 of the 15 possible pairs. Three pairs are formed, not one.
You divided by 6 people. The first person has 5 possible partners.

feedback.correct: Your partner is one of the other 5, each equally likely.
feedback.generic: Fix the first named person. Who is their partner?

explain.text: The first named person's partner is equally likely to be any of the other 5. So the chance it is the second named person is $\tfrac15$. Check: there are 15 pairings, and 3 of them pair the two.

items.title: A die sets the tosses
items.question: Roll a fair die, then toss a fair coin as many times as the die shows. What is the chance of exactly one head?

options.why: You used one typical roll of 3. Average over all six rolls.
You counted only a roll of 1.
You gave every roll the chance $\tfrac12$. With $k$ tosses it is $\tfrac{k}{2^k}$.

feedback.generic: Condition on the die, then average.

explain.text: Given $k$ tosses, exactly one head has chance $\tfrac{k}{2^k}$: $\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac38, \tfrac14, \tfrac{5}{32}, \tfrac{3}{32}$. Their sum is $\tfrac{60}{32}$, and $\tfrac16$ of that is $\tfrac{5}{16}$. Check: listing all $6 \times 64$ equally weighted cases gives the same.

items.title: Who gets more heads
items.question: You and a friend each toss 3 fair coins. What is the chance that you get more heads than your friend?

options.why: You ignored ties. A tie happens with chance $\tfrac{5}{16}$.
That is the chance of a tie.
That is the chance you get at least as many.

feedback.correct: A tie has chance $\tfrac{20}{64}$; the rest splits evenly.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of a tie first, then use symmetry.

explain.text: A tie at $k$ heads has chance $\binom3k^2 / 64$, and $1 + 9 + 9 + 1 = 20$. By symmetry you win half of the rest: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac{44}{64} = \tfrac{11}{32}$. Check: counting the 64 pairs directly gives 22 wins.

items.title: Ahead of one
items.question: Three people each draw a different random number. You learn that A's number beats B's. What is the chance that A has the highest of the three?

options.why: You ignored the news. Before it, each person is highest with chance $\tfrac13$.
You treated A versus C as all that matters, but A beating B already helps.
That is the chance of the single order A, B, C.

feedback.correct: Of the 3 orders with A above B, A is top in 2.
feedback.generic: List the orders of the three that keep A above B.

explain.text: The 6 orders are equally likely, and 3 have A above B: A, B, C; A, C, B; C, A, B. A is highest in 2 of them, so $\tfrac23$. Check: $P(\text{A top}) / P(\text{A above B}) = \tfrac13 \div \tfrac12 = \tfrac23$.

items.title: A pick inside a pick
items.question: A number $X$ is picked at random from 1, 2 and 3. Then a number is picked at random from 1 to $X$. What is the chance that this second number is 1?

options.why: You picked straight from 1 to 3. The first pick shrinks the range.
You used only the middle case, $X = 2$.
That is the chance that $X$ was 3, given the second number is 1.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac13 \left(1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13\right) = \tfrac{11}{18}$.
feedback.generic: Condition on $X$, then average.

explain.text: Given $X = 1, 2, 3$, the second number is 1 with chance $1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13$. Averaging gives $\tfrac13 \times \tfrac{11}{6} = \tfrac{11}{18}$. Check: weight the 6 end results by $\tfrac13 \times \tfrac1X$; those with 1 carry $\tfrac{6 + 3 + 2}{18}$.

items.title: Does the line die out
items.question: A cell splits into two with chance $\tfrac23$, or dies with chance $\tfrac13$. Every new cell does the same, independently. Starting from one cell, what is the chance that the line dies out?

options.why: That is only the chance it dies at the first step.
You took the other root of $q = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 q^2$. The chance is the smaller root.
That is the chance of a split, not of dying out.

feedback.correct: $q = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 q^2$ has roots $\tfrac12$ and 1; take $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Condition on the first step: dying out needs both new lines to die.

explain.text: Condition on the first step: $q = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 q^2$, so $2q^2 - 3q + 1 = 0$ and $q = \tfrac12$ or 1. Each cell has on average $\tfrac43$ children, above 1, so the line may last and $q = \tfrac12$. Check: iterating from $q = 0$ gives $\tfrac13$, 0.407, 0.44 and so on towards 0.5.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: A random point inside a circle lies more than 0.6 of the radius from its centre
A random point inside a circle lies less than 0.7 of the radius from its centre
A random point inside a circle lies less than half the radius from its centre

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.640, 0.490, 0.250.
feedback.generic: Area grows as the square of the radius, so a share of the radius is not the chance.

explain.text: More than 0.6 of the radius from the centre: $1 - 0.6^2 = 0.640$. Less than 0.7 of the radius: $0.7^2 = 0.490$. Less than half the radius: $0.5^2 = 0.250$.

items.title: Rank three events
items.prose: In a round robin, every player meets every other player once. Each game is won by either player with chance $\tfrac12$, independently.
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: With 4 players, someone wins all their games
With 4 players, someone wins all their games and someone loses all theirs
With 3 players, each player wins exactly one game

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.500, 0.375, 0.250.
feedback.generic: Two players cannot both win every game, and the top and bottom players share a game.

explain.text: Only one player can win every game, so with 4 players the chance is $4 \times \tfrac18 = 0.500$. For a top and a bottom player there are $4 \times 3$ choices, and 5 games must go their way: $\tfrac{12}{32} = 0.375$. With 3 players, each wins one game when the games form a cycle, 2 of the 8 results: 0.250.

items.title: Rank three events
items.prose: Each entry of a 2 by 2 matrix is 0 or 1, by a fair coin toss for each.
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: The matrix equals its own transpose

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.500, 0.375, 0.125.
feedback.generic: Most 0 and 1 matrices have no inverse: the determinant $ad - bc$ must be 1 or $-1$.

explain.text: It equals its transpose when its two off-diagonal entries match: 0.500. It has an inverse when exactly one of $ad$ and $bc$ is 1: $2 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac34 = 0.375$. All four entries are equal in 2 of the 16 cases: 0.125.

items.title: Rank three events
items.prose: A domino is drawn at random from a full double-six set: 28 tiles, one for each pair of ends from 0 to 6, doubles included.
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Its two ends total at least 7
Its two ends differ by at least 3

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.429, 0.357, 0.250.
feedback.generic: Count the 28 tiles, not ordered pairs of ends: each double is one tile.

explain.text: The ends total at least 7 on 6 + 4 + 2 = 12 of the 28 tiles, counting by the larger end 6, 5 and 4: 0.429. They differ by at least 3 on 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 tiles: 0.357. It is a double on 7 tiles: 0.250.

items.title: Rank three events
items.prose: Two different diagonals of a regular polygon are picked at random.
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: In a pentagon, the two diagonals cross inside it
In a hexagon, the two diagonals cross inside it
In a heptagon, the two diagonals cross inside it

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.500, 0.417, 0.385.
feedback.generic: More diagonals do not make a crossing more likely. Count sets of four corners.

explain.text: Any four corners give exactly one pair of crossing diagonals. A pentagon has 5 diagonals and 5 sets of four corners, so $\tfrac{5}{10} = 0.500$. A hexagon gives $\tfrac{15}{36} = 0.417$ and a heptagon $\tfrac{35}{91} = 0.385$.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a single game
A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a best-of-7 match
A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a best-of-3 match

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.608, 0.575, 0.550.
feedback.generic: Do not assume the three tie because the game chance is the same.

explain.text: A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a best-of-7 match: 0.608. A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a best-of-3 match: 0.575. A side that wins each game with chance 0.55 wins a single game: 0.550.

items.title: Seconds in a week
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds the number of seconds in a week.

options.why: This holds the value, but 600,000 to 610,000 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 604,800.
This sits wholly above the value, 604,800.

feedback.correct: 600,000 to 610,000 holds the value, 604,800, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $7 \times 24 = 168$ hours, and $168 \times 3600 = 604{,}800$ seconds. That sits between 600,000 and 610,000. The interval 500,000 to 700,000 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Four half-numbers
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $1.5 \times 2.5 \times 3.5 \times 4.5$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 59 to 60 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 59.06.
This sits wholly above the value, 59.06.

feedback.correct: 59 to 60 holds the value, 59.06, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: Pair the ends: $1.5 \times 4.5 = 6.75$ and $2.5 \times 3.5 = 8.75$. Then $6.75 \times 8.75 = 59.06$, just above 59. The interval 55 to 65 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Two reciprocals
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $\dfrac{1}{0.97} + \dfrac{1}{1.03}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 2.001 to 2.002 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 2.0018.
This sits wholly above the value, 2.0018.

feedback.correct: 2.001 to 2.002 holds the value, 2.0018, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: The series ends in 4, 5, 6 or 7 games with chances $\tfrac{2}{16}, \tfrac{4}{16}, \tfrac{5}{16}, \tfrac{5}{16}$. The mean is $\tfrac{8 + 20 + 30 + 35}{16} = \tfrac{93}{16} = 5.81$. The interval 5 to 6 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.
